lesson.menu_title: London, and What It Costs to Live There

lesson.grammar_point: comparatives with adverbs of degree and quantifiers

paras: Every year a few thousand people move to London on a salary that looked generous on the offer letter and turns out to be slightly less than the city needs. The number itself is not the problem. The problem is that almost nothing in London costs what the equivalent thing costs anywhere else, and the differences are not evenly spread: some things are far more expensive than people expect, a few are considerably cheaper, and one thing — housing — is so much more expensive than everything else that it quietly decides the rest of your life there.

Start with the deposit. A tenancy usually asks for five or six weeks of rent up front, held until you leave, plus the first month in advance. That is a great deal of money to find in the same week as a flight, and it is the moment most people discover that their take-home pay is a good deal smaller than the salary they agreed to. Income tax and national insurance come off before anything else, and the disposable income left at the end is the only number that ever mattered.

Then there is the trade-off nobody explains in advance, which is space against time. The further out you live, the more room you get and the longer you commute, and the two do not move at the same speed: twenty minutes further out buys you slightly more space, while forty minutes further out buys you a great deal more. Nearly everybody underestimates how much of their week the journey takes, and hardly anybody moves back in once they have somewhere to put their books. Utilities are higher than in Brazil, food is roughly comparable, and public transport is expensive but so much better than driving that the comparison is not really a comparison.

So is it worth it? Most people who stay say yes, and most of them are not paying for a family. That is the honest version of the answer. The professional opportunity is genuinely larger, the salaries in law and finance are far higher than almost anywhere in Europe, and there is considerably more of everything to do than you will ever get through. It is also a city where a great many people scrape by on incomes that sounded enormous when they accepted them, and where whole neighbourhoods have been priced out in a single decade. Both things are true at once, and anybody who tells you only one of them is selling something.

listenings.text: The offer looked enormous. I remember converting it in my head on the train home and thinking that we would be considerably better off than in Sao Paulo. What I had not converted was anything else. Tax and national insurance took a much larger bite than I expected, so the take-home pay was already a good deal smaller than the number I had been celebrating. Then the deposit: six weeks of rent, held, plus the first month, in the same fortnight as two flights and a shipping container. For the first three months we scraped by on a salary that in Portuguese sounds like a lot of money. It got better, and I would do it again, but I would tell anybody moving to work out the disposable income first and ignore the headline entirely. The headline is the one number that never touches your life.

I have placed people in this city for eleven years, and the conversation that decides whether somebody stays is never about salary. It is about the trade-off between space and time. People move further out because the flats are far bigger and the rent is a little lower, and they underestimate the commute every single time. Twenty minutes further out is nothing, and it buys you slightly more room. Forty minutes further out is a different life: it is nearly seven hours a week, which is far more than anybody budgets for, and it is the hours at both ends of the day, which are the ones that matter. My advice is unfashionable. Take the smaller flat closer in for the first year, find out where your life actually happens, and move once you know. Moving twice is expensive. Commuting for two years is much more expensive, and you pay for it in something you cannot get back.
